summary: This program defines a small named block of code called a method (Java's word for a function) and runs it twice from main. It shows how naming a piece of work lets you reuse it without repeating the instructions.

lines.text: Every Java program lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name, so this code belongs in IntroFunction.java.
This is the entry point: when you run the class, Java looks for exactly this method signature and starts here.
Calling the method by name runs the code in its body; the empty parentheses mean it needs no information passed in.
The same call a second time proves the real value of a method: one definition, as many uses as you like.
This defines the method. The word void says it hands nothing back to the caller, and static means it belongs to the class itself, so main can call it directly.
This is the single piece of work the method exists to do, which is why you see the message printed twice when the program runs.
